title: Paper 1 Question 4 The Examiner’s Answer
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles works through a deliberately weak answer written by a senior examiner for the June 2023 Life of Pi evaluation question, then through the same examiner's full mark answer, to show what the mark scheme actually rewards. His argument is that the standard classroom advice, write four paragraphs and use sophisticated vocabulary, explains nothing, since the examiner's own grade 3 answer does both and still fails. He reads the official examiner commentary as unhelpful because it praises focus and evidence at length and reduces the real problem to the phrase not specific enough. In its place he offers his Points Make Prizes rule, that a mark is earned by each valid explanation, defined as an explanation tied to a quote from the correct section of the text, aimed at the question's focus, and not repeating an earlier point. He then annotates both answers line by line, scoring the weak response at 10 marks and showing which sentences earn nothing, and notes that the number of marks available tells a student exactly how many valid explanations to produce. The piece doubles as a critique of an assessment regime where a student can answer the question fully and still be told it is not enough.
points: The teaching move is to annotate a deliberately weak answer sentence by sentence, marking which lines earn a mark and which earn zero and why.
Salles argues paragraph count and vocabulary are red herrings, since the examiner's own grade 3 answer is nearly 400 words with adult level diction.
He translates the mark scheme phrase not specific enough into a testable rule, that an explanation must be anchored to a quote or paraphrase from the right section.
Because each valid explanation earns one mark, the tariff on the question doubles as a target for how many explanations to write.
Comparing the two answers shows the full mark response uses 14 quotes, some with several distinct explanations attached to the same quote.
quotes: This answer was written by the senior examiner. See if you can work out why it only gets a grade 3.

The vocabulary in this answer is way beyond anything a real grade 3 student would write - but it still gets grade 3. That is a fantastic clue that your vocabulary is not what is getting you the grade.
Answering the question fully - which this answer does - is not enough to get a grade 4!
It is the number of valid explanations you write which gives you the number of marks.
The number of marks in the question tells you exactly how many valid explanations to write.
Clearly, this ‘student’ has a great understanding of the text. They could easily have got a grade 7 if they just knew what a valid explanation was.
There are 14 quotes. So the senior examiner finds some quotes to zoom in on, focusing on short phrases, and some quotes with more than one explanation.
